chapter.title: Scaling building blocks
chapter.summary: Load balancing, caching and rate limiting: the pieces every large system is assembled from, each as a high-level design and as code.

lessons.title: Load balancing
lessons.summary: Spreading traffic across many servers: algorithms, layers, health checks, and a pluggable balancer in code.

parts.label: HLD
parts.body:
## Why a load balancer

One server has a ceiling: CPU, memory, network. You can **scale up** (a bigger machine, simple, but there is a limit and one failure kills you) or **scale out** (more machines behind a **load balancer (LB)**). Scaling out gives capacity *and* availability: if one server dies, the LB stops sending it traffic.

```
clients -> DNS -> [Load balancer] -> server 1 / server 2 / server 3
```

The LB is the single entry point, so it must not become a single point of failure: run **at least two** (active-active or active-passive with a floating IP / DNS failover).

## Layer 4 vs Layer 7

| | L4 (transport) | L7 (application) |
|---|---|---|
| Sees | IP, port, TCP/UDP | HTTP path, headers, cookies, TLS contents |
| Speed | Very fast, little state | Slower, can terminate TLS and inspect |
| Can do | Spread connections | Route `/api` vs `/static`, A/B, auth, rate limit, retries |
| Examples | AWS NLB, HAProxy tcp mode | AWS ALB, Nginx, Envoy |

Use L7 when you need content-aware routing (microservices, canary releases). Use L4 for raw throughput or non-HTTP protocols.

## Algorithms

- **Round robin**: servers in turn. Simple; ignores load and server size.
- **Weighted round robin**: bigger machines get proportionally more.
- **Least connections**: send to the server with the fewest active connections. Good when requests vary in duration (websockets, uploads).
- **Least response time**: fastest recent responder.
- **IP hash / consistent hash**: same client (or key) goes to the same server. Gives **stickiness** for in-memory sessions or cache locality. Consistent hashing keeps most keys in place when a server is added or removed.
- **Power of two choices**: pick two random servers, send to the less loaded. Surprisingly close to optimal with almost no coordination.

## Health checks and failure handling

The LB probes each server (`GET /health` every few seconds). After N consecutive failures it marks the server **out of rotation**; after M successes it is back. Use **passive** checks too: eject on repeated 5xx or timeouts. Add **connection draining** so in-flight requests finish when a server is deployed or removed.

## Stateless servers and sessions

Load balancing is easy only if servers are **stateless**: any server can handle any request. Keep session data in a shared store (Redis) or a signed token (JWT), not in process memory. If you must use sticky sessions, remember a restart or scale-in drops those sessions.

## Beyond one data centre

- **DNS / GeoDNS** sends users to the nearest region.
- **Global load balancers / anycast** route to healthy regions.
- Inside a region, an L4 LB fronts a fleet of L7 proxies, which front the services. This tiering is how very large sites scale the LB itself.

## Trade-offs to mention in an interview

- LB adds a hop of latency and is infrastructure to operate (use managed ones where possible).
- TLS termination at the LB offloads work but means traffic behind it may be plain text, so secure the internal network or re-encrypt.
- Sticky sessions simplify state but unbalance load and hurt failover.
- Autoscaling needs the LB to discover new instances (service registry or cloud target groups).

flowchart TD
  U["Clients"] --> D["DNS / GeoDNS"]
  D --> L1["Load balancer A"]
  D --> L2["Load balancer B (standby)"]
  L1 --> S1["Server 1"]
  L1 --> S2["Server 2"]
  L1 --> S3["Server 3"]

  L2 --> S2
  L2 --> S3
  S1 --> R[("Shared session store: Redis")]
  S2 --> R
  S3 --> R

parts.label: LLD
parts.body:
## What the interviewer wants

"Design a load balancer class": a component that holds a set of servers, picks one per request using an **interchangeable algorithm**, and skips unhealthy servers. The classic answer uses the **Strategy pattern**.

## Entities

- `Server { id, weight, healthy, activeConnections }`
- `LoadBalancingStrategy` (interface): `pick(servers, key?) -> Server`
- Implementations: `RoundRobin`, `LeastConnections`, `ConsistentHash` (Strategy pattern)
- `LoadBalancer`: owns the server list and a strategy, filters to healthy servers, delegates `pick`. Exposes `addServer`, `removeServer`, `setHealth`, `route(request)`.

## Why Strategy

The algorithm varies independently of everything else. With the strategy behind an interface, you add a new algorithm without touching `LoadBalancer`, and tests can swap in a deterministic one. This is the **Open/Closed Principle** in practice.

## Concurrency

A real LB handles many requests at once. Round robin needs an **atomic counter** (or a lock) so two threads do not read the same index. Server list changes (add/remove) should be copy-on-write or guarded by a read-write lock so a pick never sees a half-updated list.

## Extension points to mention

- Health checker as a separate class that calls `setHealth` (Observer or a scheduled task).
- Connection draining: mark a server `draining` so it receives no new requests.
- Weighted round robin: expand servers by weight, or use smooth weighted round robin.
- Metrics: counters per server for observability.

## Edge cases

No healthy servers (return an error, do not loop forever), a server removed mid-request, integer overflow of the round-robin counter (use modulo and wrap), and a key-based strategy when the server list changes.

diagrams.title: Strategy pattern: the balancer depends on an interface
diagrams.code:
classDiagram
  class LoadBalancer {
    -servers
    -strategy
    +addServer(s)
    +removeServer(id)
    +route(key)
  }
  class Strategy {
    <<interface>>
    +pick(servers, key)
  }
  class RoundRobin
  class LeastConnections
  class ConsistentHash
  LoadBalancer o-- Strategy
  Strategy <|.. RoundRobin
  Strategy <|.. LeastConnections
  Strategy <|.. ConsistentHash

keyPoints: A load balancer gives capacity and availability, so run at least two and keep servers stateless.
L4 balances connections quickly; L7 understands HTTP and enables routing, retries and TLS termination.
Pick the algorithm for the workload: round robin for uniform requests, least connections for uneven ones.
Health checks and connection draining keep failures and deploys invisible to users.
In LLD, put each algorithm behind a Strategy interface and make the round-robin counter thread-safe.

check.q: Which load balancing method suits long-lived, uneven requests such as websockets?
check.why: Least connections accounts for how busy each server currently is, which round robin ignores.

check.q: Why should the app servers behind a load balancer be stateless?
options: Any server can serve any request, so scaling and failover are trivial
Load balancers cannot route stateful traffic
check.why: If session state lives in a shared store, requests are interchangeable across servers.

check.q: In the LLD, why is the balancing algorithm an interface?
options: So algorithms can be swapped without changing LoadBalancer (Strategy / Open-Closed)
check.why: The varying part is isolated behind an interface so new strategies need no changes to the balancer.

lessons.title: Caching
lessons.summary: Where to cache, write strategies, eviction, and the classic failure modes, then an LRU cache in code.

parts.label: HLD
parts.body:
## Why cache

Reading from memory takes about **100 nanoseconds**; a database query takes **milliseconds**, 10,000 to 100,000 times slower. Many reads ask for the same popular data. Caching keeps hot data close so you serve it fast and spare the database.

## Where caches live

1. **Client / browser cache**: HTTP `Cache-Control`, `ETag`. Free and closest to the user.
2. **CDN**: caches static (and some dynamic) content near users worldwide.
3. **API gateway / reverse proxy cache**: whole responses.
4. **Application (in-process) cache**: a map in each server. Fastest, but every instance has its own copy, so it can disagree.
5. **Distributed cache** (Redis, Memcached): a shared cache tier all servers use.
6. **Database cache**: buffer pool, query cache.

## Read strategies

**Cache-aside (lazy loading)**: the most common.

```
read(key):
  v = cache.get(key)
  if v is hit: return v
  v = db.read(key)
  cache.set(key, v, ttl)
  return v
```

Simple and resilient (cache down means slower, not broken). Downside: first read is a miss, and data can be stale.

**Read-through**: the cache itself loads from the DB on a miss.

## Write strategies

| Strategy | How | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Write-through** | write to cache and DB together | consistent, no loss | slower writes, caches data never read |
| **Write-back (write-behind)** | write to cache, flush to DB later | very fast writes | data loss if the cache dies before flush |
| **Write-around** | write to DB only; cache fills on read | avoids polluting cache | first read after write is a miss |
| **Invalidate on write** (with cache-aside) | write DB, then delete the key | simple, common | race windows (see below) |

## Eviction

When the cache is full, something must go: **LRU** (least recently used, the default choice), **LFU** (least frequently used), **FIFO**, **TTL** (expire after a time), random. TTL also bounds staleness.

## The hard part: invalidation and failure modes

- **Stale data**: DB updated but cache not. Use short TTLs and delete-on-write; accept eventual consistency where the product allows.
- **Cache stampede (thundering herd)**: a hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the DB at once. Fixes: **request coalescing** (one loader, others wait), **jittered TTLs**, refresh-ahead, locks with a short timeout.
- **Cache penetration**: lookups for keys that never exist bypass the cache every time. Fix: cache negative results briefly, or use a **Bloom filter** in front.
- **Hot keys**: one key overloads a single cache node. Fix: replicate hot keys or add a local cache in front.
- **Cache avalanche**: many keys expire together. Fix: randomise TTLs.

## Scaling the cache tier

Partition keys across cache nodes with **consistent hashing** so adding or removing a node moves few keys. Add replicas for availability. Know that a cold cache after a restart can melt the database: warm it or rate-limit refills.

## What to cache

Read-heavy, expensive-to-compute, tolerant of slight staleness: profiles, product pages, feed fragments, computed aggregates, sessions. Do **not** cache data that must be strongly consistent (account balances during a transfer).

## Metrics

Watch **hit ratio** (aim for 90%+ on hot paths), latency, evictions, memory. A low hit ratio means the cache is too small, keys are poorly chosen or TTLs are too short.

diagrams.title: Cache-aside read path
diagrams.code:
flowchart TD
  A["App receives read"] --> B{"In cache?"}
  B -- "hit" --> C["Return value"]
  B -- "miss" --> D["Read from database"]
  D --> E["Store in cache with TTL"]
  E --> C

parts.label: LLD
parts.body:
## The classic: design an LRU cache

**Requirements**: fixed capacity; `get(key)` and `put(key, value)` both in **O(1)**; when full, evict the **least recently used** item. Both reads and writes count as a "use".

## The key insight

You need two things at once: **fast lookup by key** (hash map) and **fast reordering by recency** (a list where you can move a node to the front and remove from the back in O(1)). A singly linked list cannot remove a node in O(1) without its predecessor, so use a **doubly linked list**.

- `HashMap<key, Node>`: finds a node in O(1).
- `DoublyLinkedList`: head = most recent, tail = least recent.
- `get`: look up the node, move it to the head, return its value.
- `put`: if present, update and move to head. If new, create a node at the head; if over capacity, remove the tail and delete its key from the map.

Use **sentinel head and tail nodes** so there are no null checks at the ends.

## Class design

- `Node { key, value, prev, next }`: store the **key** in the node so eviction can delete the map entry.
- `LRUCache(capacity)`: `get`, `put`, plus private `remove(node)` and `addToFront(node)`.

## Making it production-grade

- **Thread safety**: guard with a lock (a single mutex is fine; reads mutate order, so a read lock is not enough), or shard the cache into N segments by key hash to reduce contention.
- **TTL**: store an expiry per node; check on `get`; optionally a background sweeper.
- **Eviction policy as a Strategy**: `EvictionPolicy` interface with `LRU`, `LFU`, `FIFO` implementations so the cache is policy-agnostic.
- **Generics**: `Cache<K, V>`.
- **Observability**: hit/miss counters.

## Edge cases

Capacity of 1, `put` of an existing key (must not grow size), `get` of a missing key, capacity 0, null values vs missing.

diagrams.title: LRU = hash map + doubly linked list
diagrams.code:
flowchart LR
  M["HashMap: key to node"] -.-> N2
  H["head sentinel"] <--> N1["most recent"] <--> N2["..."] <--> N3["least recent"] <--> T["tail sentinel"]

keyPoints: Cache hot, read-heavy, staleness-tolerant data; cache-aside is the default pattern.
Write-through is consistent, write-back is fast but can lose data, write-around avoids pollution.
Invalidate on write and use TTLs with jitter to bound staleness and avoid avalanches.
Stampede, penetration and hot keys are the classic failure modes, each with a known fix.
LRU = hash map + doubly linked list with sentinels, giving O(1) get and put.

check.q: Why does an LRU cache need a doubly (not singly) linked list?
options: Doubly linked lists use less memory
Removing an arbitrary node in O(1) needs its predecessor pointer
Singly linked lists cannot hold keys
It makes the hash map unnecessary
check.why: When a node is accessed it is removed from the middle and moved to the front; that needs prev and next to be O(1).

check.q: A very popular key expires and thousands of requests hit the database together. This is a:
check.why: Many concurrent misses for one hot key is a stampede; coalescing requests or refreshing ahead fixes it.

check.q: Which write strategy risks losing data if the cache crashes before flushing?
check.why: Write-back acknowledges the write from the cache and persists later, so unflushed writes are lost on a crash.

lessons.title: Rate limiting
lessons.summary: Protecting a service from overload and abuse: the four algorithms, distributed enforcement, and a token bucket in code.

parts.label: HLD
parts.body:
## Why rate limit

A **rate limiter** caps how many requests a client may make in a window. It protects against abuse and bots, prevents one noisy tenant from starving others, controls cost (paid downstream APIs), and shields the system from overload (a form of **load shedding**).

## Where it runs

- **API gateway / edge** (most common): one place, before requests reach services.
- **In the service** (middleware): finer control, per-endpoint.
- **Client side** (cooperative): the SDK backs off, but you cannot trust it.

On rejection return **HTTP 429 Too Many Requests** with headers `Retry-After`, `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `X-RateLimit-Reset`.

## What to limit by

User id, API key, IP address, tenant, or endpoint. Combine: e.g. 100/min per user *and* 1000/min per IP. IP alone is unfair behind a shared NAT.

## The four algorithms

**1. Token bucket** (most popular). A bucket holds up to `capacity` tokens and refills at `rate` tokens/second. Each request takes one token; if none, reject. **Allows bursts** up to capacity but enforces the long-run average rate. Memory: 2 numbers per key.

**2. Leaky bucket.** Requests enter a queue that drains at a fixed rate. Smooths traffic to a constant output; bursts overflow and are dropped. Good when downstream needs a steady rate.

**3. Fixed window counter.** Count requests per clock window (e.g. per minute). Simple and cheap, but a burst straddling the boundary can send **2× the limit** in a short span (end of one window plus start of the next).

**4. Sliding window.** Fixes the boundary issue.
- *Sliding log*: store each request timestamp. Exact, but memory-heavy.
- *Sliding window counter*: weight the previous window's count by overlap: `count = prev × (1 - elapsed%) + current`. Approximate, tiny memory.

| Algorithm | Bursts | Memory | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Token bucket | allowed | tiny | good |
| Leaky bucket | smoothed | queue | good |
| Fixed window | boundary spikes | tiny | poor at edges |
| Sliding log | none | high | exact |
| Sliding counter | small error | tiny | very good |

## Distributed rate limiting

With many gateway nodes, per-node counters let a client multiply their limit. Options:

- **Central store (Redis)**: all nodes share counters. Use an **atomic** operation (a Lua script or `INCR` + `EXPIRE`) to avoid race conditions where two nodes both read 99 and allow the 100th and 101st.
- **Sticky routing**: send a client to one node (hurts balance).
- **Local + sync**: approximate local counters synchronised periodically; trades accuracy for latency.

Decide **fail open vs fail closed** if Redis is down: fail open keeps the product up (risking overload), fail closed protects the backend (risking an outage). Most public APIs fail open with local fallback limits.

## Other design points

- Rules live in config (hot-reloadable), keyed by endpoint and tier.
- Add **jitter and exponential backoff** guidance for clients on 429.
- Different limits per plan (free vs paid).
- Observe rejected counts per client; alert on spikes.

diagrams.title: Rate limiter at the gateway with a shared Redis counter
diagrams.code:
flowchart LR
  C["Client"] --> G["API gateway: rate limiter"]
  G -- "check and decrement atomically" --> R[("Redis")]
  G -- "allowed" --> S["Service"]
  G -- "rejected" --> X["429 + Retry-After"]

parts.label: LLD
parts.body:
## Design a rate limiter class

**Requirements**: `allow(clientId) -> boolean`; configurable limit; thread-safe; pluggable algorithm; many clients.

## Entities

- `RateLimiter` (interface): `allow(key): boolean`
- `TokenBucketLimiter`, `FixedWindowLimiter`, `SlidingWindowLimiter` (Strategy)
- `Bucket { tokens, lastRefill }`: per-key state
- `RateLimiterFactory` to build the right one from config

## Token bucket without a timer thread

Don't run a background thread refilling every bucket. **Refill lazily**: on each request compute how much time passed since `lastRefill`, add `elapsed × rate` tokens (capped at capacity), then try to take one.

```
allow(key):
  b = buckets[key] or new Bucket(capacity, now)
  elapsed = now - b.lastRefill
  b.tokens = min(capacity, b.tokens + elapsed * ratePerSec)
  b.lastRefill = now
  if b.tokens >= 1: b.tokens -= 1; return true
  return false
```

O(1) per request, O(1) memory per client.

## Concurrency

The read-refill-decrement sequence must be **atomic per key**. Use a lock per bucket (or `ConcurrentHashMap.compute`), not a global lock. In a distributed version, this exact logic runs as one **Redis Lua script**.

## Memory

Idle clients accumulate buckets forever. Evict buckets idle longer than `capacity / rate` (they are full again anyway), with a periodic sweep or an LRU map.

## Testability

Inject a **clock** (`now()` function) instead of calling `Date.now()` inside, so tests can advance time deterministically.

## Edge cases

Clock going backwards (clamp elapsed to ≥ 0), fractional tokens, first request for a new key, limit changes at runtime, and burst capacity larger than the per-second rate.

diagrams.title: Token bucket refill and consume
diagrams.code:
flowchart TD
  A["Request arrives"] --> B["Refill tokens from elapsed time, cap at capacity"]
  B --> C{"tokens >= 1?"}
  C -- "yes" --> D["tokens = tokens - 1: allow"]
  C -- "no" --> E["reject: 429"]

code.source:
import threading, time

class TokenBucketLimiter:
    def __init__(self, capacity, refill_per_sec, clock=time.monotonic):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.rate = refill_per_sec
        self.clock = clock
        self._buckets = {}          # key -> [tokens, last]
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def allow(self, key) -> bool:
        now = self.clock()
        with self._lock:            # atomic read-refill-consume
            tokens, last = self._buckets.get(key, (self.capacity, now))
            tokens = min(self.capacity, tokens + max(0, now - last) * self.rate)
            allowed = tokens >= 1
            if allowed:
                tokens -= 1
            self._buckets[key] = (tokens, now)
            return allowed

keyPoints: Return 429 with Retry-After; limit by user, key, IP or tenant, often several at once.
Token bucket allows bursts at a steady average; fixed window has boundary spikes; sliding window fixes them.
Distributed limiting needs an atomic shared counter, such as a Redis Lua script.
Refill lazily from elapsed time instead of running a timer thread per bucket.
Inject a clock for tests and clean up idle buckets to bound memory.

check.q: What is the main flaw of the fixed window counter?
options: It uses a lot of memory
A burst across a window boundary can allow up to twice the limit
check.why: Requests at the end of one window and the start of the next both count against fresh windows.

check.q: Why refill a token bucket lazily on each request rather than with a timer?
options: Timers are not allowed in production
It needs no background work and is O(1) per request and per key
It avoids the need for locks
check.why: Computing tokens from elapsed time gives the same result without a thread per bucket.

check.q: Two gateway nodes both read a counter of 99 and both allow a request. What prevents this?
options: An atomic check-and-increment in the shared store (for example a Lua script)
check.why: The read, check and write must be one atomic operation so concurrent nodes cannot both pass.
